unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7 of your Year 8 English course. In this unit, you will explore the theme of Historical Figures and Legacy -- a topic that invites you to think about how individuals shape history and how their actions echo through generations. The centrepiece is an original story, "The Rebellion of Silence", which follows Jamal, a quiet but determined student at an East African boarding school in 1948, as his anonymous essays challenge an unjust ban on debate. Alongside the story, you will master the grammar of narrating the past -- Past Simple and Past Continuous, the Past Perfect, reported speech, verbs with prepositions, phrasal verbs, reflexive pronouns, time phrases and discourse markers -- and build a rich vocabulary for discussing argument, leadership, emotion and change.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

readings.title: Legacy: The People History Remembers
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
What turns an ordinary person into a historical figure? The easy answer is fame: the faces printed in textbooks, the leaders whose statues stand in city squares. The harder and more interesting answer is legacy -- the mark a person leaves on other people, which continues working long after that person has gone. Judged by legacy, a historical figure does not have to be famous at all. A teacher who trains a generation of writers, a nurse who reorganises a clinic, or a student who starts a discussion club can shape a community as surely as any general.
The words such people choose also shape how change is received. A petulant complaint is easy for those in power to dismiss, but an emphatic, carefully justified argument is not. Writers and speakers through history have understood that the tone of a sentence can open a door that shouting would slam shut.
Consider East Africa in the late 1940s, the setting of this unit's story. Most of the region was still governed as European colonies, and many schools, offices and newspapers were controlled by colonial authorities. Yet change was already moving. Radios crackled with news and speeches from Nairobi, Accra and Dar es Salaam, carrying arguments across borders faster than any newspaper cart could travel. Returning soldiers, market traders and young teachers asked pointed questions about fairness, taxation and representation. By 1948, whispers of independence were spreading from town to town, although few people could have predicted how quickly the political map would change over the following twenty years.
Institutions rarely welcome such questions. A conservative headmaster, trained to value order above debate, might see silence as safety and treat every pamphlet as a threat. A more liberal school board might argue the opposite: that a school which forbids questions produces obedient pupils but weak thinkers. Between these two positions sits the student, who must decide whether to comply, to argue openly, or to act quietly and let results speak. History offers many examples of that third path. Petitions copied by hand, essays passed from reader to reader, and small savings clubs that funded scholarships were rarely dramatic. Yet they were patient and systematic, and their effects accumulated year after year. Quiet initiative of this kind is easy for rulers to underestimate, which is precisely why it so often succeeds.
How should we judge such figures today? Historians begin with sources: letters, school records, newspapers, photographs and the memories of witnesses. Each source carries a viewpoint. A colonial newspaper might describe a student protest as childish mischief, while a participant's diary might describe the same event as an act of profound courage. Neither account is automatically reliable. The historian's task is to compare them, to ask who wrote each one and why, and to reach a conclusion that the surviving evidence can justify. When sources disagree, the disagreement is itself information: it tells us the event mattered enough to argue about.
Legacy, finally, is measured in people rather than monuments. The clearest sign that a person changed history is that others continued the work: students who kept writing after the first writer left, readers who became speakers, and speakers who became teachers. As you read "The Rebellion of Silence", keep this test in mind. Ask not only what the main character does, but who follows him, and which habits of courage survive at the school after his year group has gone. That is where a legacy truly lives.

readings.title: The Storyteller's Toolkit: Talking About the Past
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every story about the past depends on a small toolkit of grammar, and this unit teaches you to handle eight of its tools with confidence. None of them is decoration. Each one answers a question that a reader silently asks: What happened? What was already happening? What happened first? Who said what? The better you control these tools, the more clearly your reader can see the events you describe.
The first two tools work as a pair. The Past Simple reports a completed action: Jamal wrote an essay. The school banned debate. You form it with -ed for regular verbs, or with special forms such as went, wrote and found for irregular ones. The Past Continuous, built from was or were with an -ing verb, stretches an action across time: Jamal was writing. The students were whispering. Combined, the pair lets one action interrupt another: Jamal was writing an essay when the prefect found his notebook. While the students were playing football, Jamal slipped behind the assembly hall. Storytellers rely on this combination constantly, because real events rarely happen politely one at a time.
The third tool reaches further back. The Past Perfect, formed with had and a past participle, shows which of two past events happened first: By the time the headmaster arrived, Jamal had already hidden his notebook. Without it, your reader must guess the order of events; with it, the timeline becomes crystal clear.
The fourth tool is reported speech. When you retell what someone said without quoting the exact words, you shift the tense one step back, adjust the pronouns, and drop the question mark. If Tariq said, "We need to keep this going", you would report it as: Tariq said that they needed to keep it going. Questions take asked with if or whether, and commands take told with to: The headmaster told the students to focus on their studies.
Three smaller tools govern individual words. Certain verbs demand a particular preposition: you insist on a plan, believe in an idea, waver between two choices, and implore someone for help. Phrasal verbs join a verb to a particle and create an entirely new meaning: you get on with your work, get into trouble, watch enthusiasm ebb away, or feel your emotions roil over. Reflexive pronouns step in when the subject and the object are the same person: Jamal taught himself to write persuasive essays, and the students organised the club by themselves.
The final pair of tools manages the flow of a whole text. Time phrases such as in those days, eventually, at the time and by 1948 pin each event to its place on the timeline, and they usually sit most naturally at the start of a sentence. Discourse markers such as well, basically, actually, in fact and for example guide your listener through an argument the way signposts guide a traveller, and in writing they are followed by a comma.
You will meet every one of these tools inside "The Rebellion of Silence". As you read, notice how the narrator moves between the Past Simple and the Past Continuous, how the Past Perfect signals earlier events, and how the characters' spoken words could be reported indirectly. Then reach for the same tools deliberately in your own writing and speaking this unit. A storyteller who controls time, speech and flow can make a reader believe almost anything -- which is exactly why these skills repay careful practice.

readings.title: The Rebellion of Silence, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In 1948, the stone paths of Kambazi School twisted between mango trees and unsightly dormitory blocks. The buildings bore the wear of time -- peeling paint, rusted windows -- but the minds inside them were ecstatic with questions.
Among the Form 4 students was Jamal, a boy with a quiet disposition and a habit of observing more than speaking. He kept a leather notebook in his pocket, filled with phrases, speeches, and small essays scribbled in the margins. His teachers called him bright. His classmates called him strange. But most saw him as harmless -- a benign shadow in the back row.
That was before the announcement.
The headmaster, a stiff British man with a stiff red nose, summoned the students to the courtyard. His voice boomed: "Starting next week, debate and politics will be forbidden on school grounds."
There was a long pause. Then murmurs.
"For those who do not comply," he added, "we will have no choice but to banish them."
Jamal's hand tightened around his notebook.
By 1948, whispers of independence had begun to drift across the continent like wind across long grass. Radios crackled with stories from Nairobi, Accra, and Dar es Salaam. But here, in the hills of northern Tanganyika, silence was still enforced -- through rules, expectations, and fear.
The students were instructed to focus on their studies and not "get into trouble." One evening, while others played football, Jamal slipped behind the old assembly hall. There, he found Tariq, his classmate, and three others gathered around a candle. They were sharing a cache of newspapers and pamphlets hidden in a biscuit tin.
"We need to keep this going," Tariq whispered. "Debate, writing, everything. We cannot let them take our voices."
Jamal wavered. "But what if they catch us?"
"They cannot expel us all."
Actually, they could. And they had before. But something in Tariq's voice kindled a flame inside Jamal -- something bold, profound.
"I will write," Jamal said.
He began crafting essays at night, under the blankets. One was titled The Burden of Obedience. Another: When Laws Become Shackles. His tone was cautious but emphatic, each sentence carefully justified. He used phrases like "In those days" and "Eventually, the silence will end."
He submitted the first essay anonymously, sliding it under the common room door where staff sometimes found lost items. To his surprise, it was read aloud during morning literature class.
"This is... daring," said Miss Imani, the Kiswahili teacher. She raised an eyebrow but said nothing more.
Word spread. Students began slipping quotes into conversation. Debates re-emerged -- furtive but fierce. Kambazi's silence was ebbing.
Then, during a Saturday dorm inspection, a prefect found Jamal's notebook hidden behind a loose brick. It was taken straight to the headmaster's office.
"You wrote this?" the headmaster asked the next morning, waving a sheet covered in red annotations.
Jamal nodded, trying not to waver.
The headmaster sighed. "You have caused... unrest. And now you will replenish it with order."
He assigned Jamal to write a formal apology and to clean every classroom for a week.
"But sir," Jamal began.
"No counterarguments," the headmaster snapped.
That week was strenuous. By midday each day, Jamal's arms ached. Still, he noticed things -- how quickly silence returned, and how quickly fear crept back into its old habitation.
Tariq was furious. "You should have resisted! Why didn't you make a scene?"
"I did what I had to," Jamal replied. "Resistance isn't always noise."
"Well," Tariq muttered, "your quiet rebellion isn't working."
Actually, it was.
Two days later, another essay appeared -- this time by someone else. Then another. And another. They were printed by hand and passed under desks. A network had formed, patient and systematic.

readings.title: The Rebellion of Silence, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
One night, the headmaster addressed the students in the dining hall.
"I know some of you believe in change. But this school is not a parliament. It is a place of learning."
He implored them to focus on books, not battles. But even as he spoke, the walls of silence were starting to crack.
At the term's end, the school hosted a speech contest. The headmaster considered cancelling it, but the board insisted. "It teaches confidence," they said.
Students submitted their topics in sealed envelopes. Jamal's title was simple: On the Edge of Thought.
When he stood to speak, the hall quieted.
"In those days," he began, "we believed that silence was peace. That if we obeyed, we would be safe."
He paused. "But silence is not always peace. It is sometimes the defect in freedom."
He went on, telling the story -- not by name, but clearly -- of everything that had happened. He ended with a single line: "Speech is breath made brave."
The hall clapped. The headmaster did not.
By the next week, Jamal had been called to the office again. The board was debating whether to banish him.
The headmaster stared at him. "Do you justify your actions?"
Jamal said, "I believe in learning. I believe in questions. If that is a fault, then I am guilty."
The headmaster blinked. "You are lucky the board is more liberal than I am."
Jamal left, not sure whether he had been punished or protected.
Weeks passed. The rainy season brought mud to the courtyards and dampness to the dormitories. But it also brought a new initiative: student-run discussion clubs, approved by the board under strict guidelines. The headmaster remained sceptical, but he had lost his power to roil the student body into fearful submission.
Jamal was invited to help organise the first club meeting. He declined at first, but Tariq insisted.
"You started this. You should speak."
"Well," Jamal said slowly, "maybe I will attend."
The meeting was held in the old library, a room that had once been used for storage. Now, swept clean and lined with borrowed stools, it pulsed with energy. Topics ranged from the circumference of social justice to the defects in colonial education systems. Some discussions were clumsy. Others were emphatic. Jamal noticed that students who had never raised a hand in class were suddenly leading arguments.
Even the head prefect -- a strict, conservative student named Amara -- joined the second meeting.
"I do not agree with all this liberal chatter," she said. "But I respect the courage it takes to speak."
Her presence changed everything. It gave the movement weight and credibility.
One afternoon, Jamal was called to Miss Imani's office. She greeted him with tea.
"You have done something rare," she said.
"I got into trouble," Jamal replied.
"You changed the tone of the school."
He smiled, then frowned. "But what happens after I leave?"
"That depends on who follows you."
Years later, Jamal would return to Kambazi as a visiting speaker. He would walk past the old dormitories, past the mango trees, and into the new auditorium named after Miss Imani. A portrait of her hung near the door, and the caption beneath it read: She believed in brave breath.
He stepped onto the stage. The room was packed. Students from every year sat shoulder to shoulder, eyes bright, hands full of notebooks.
He took a deep breath.
"In those days," he began, "silence was safe. But safety is not the same as freedom. And freedom does not always shout. Sometimes it waits. It listens. And then it speaks."
And speak, he did.

comprehension.question: According to the information text, how did news and speeches travel across East Africa by 1948, and from which cities?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Radios crackled with news and speeches from Nairobi, Accra and Dar es Salaam, carrying arguments across borders faster than any newspaper cart could travel.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the paragraph describing East Africa in the late 1940s.

comprehension.question: In the toolkit text, which two tenses combine in the example about Jamal writing an essay when the prefect found his notebook?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The Past Continuous (was writing) stretches the background action while the Past Simple (found) reports the action that interrupts it.
comprehension.explanation: Checks that the learner can match the toolkit's worked example to the two tenses it demonstrates.

comprehension.question: What did Jamal discover behind the old assembly hall one evening, and who was gathered there?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He found his classmate Tariq and three others around a candle, sharing a cache of newspapers and pamphlets hidden in a biscuit tin.
comprehension.explanation: A literal retrieval question anchored in the secret-group scene of part 1.

comprehension.question: What title did Jamal submit for the speech contest, and what did he call silence in his speech?
comprehension.correctAnswer: His title was On the Edge of Thought, and he told the hall that silence is not always peace but sometimes the defect in freedom.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the speech-contest scene of part 2.

comprehension.question: The writer claims a historical figure does not have to be famous. Which three examples in the opening paragraph support this claim?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The text names a teacher who trains a generation of writers, a nurse who reorganises a clinic, and a student who starts a discussion club.
comprehension.explanation: The learner must connect the writer's claim about legacy to the supporting examples that immediately follow it.

comprehension.question: According to the toolkit, what three changes do you make when you turn direct speech into reported speech?
comprehension.correctAnswer: You shift the tense one step back, adjust the pronouns, and drop the question mark when reporting a question.
comprehension.explanation: Tests understanding of the reported-speech tool as the toolkit text explains it.

comprehension.question: How does Jamal first respond to Tariq's plan, and what finally persuades him to promise to write?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He wavers and asks what will happen if they are caught, but something bold in Tariq's voice kindles a flame inside him, so he says he will write.

comprehension.question: The text argues that quiet initiative is easy for rulers to underestimate, which is precisely why it so often succeeds. Evaluate this claim using two historical examples from the passage.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Hand-copied petitions, essays passed from reader to reader, and savings clubs that funded scholarships were rarely dramatic, yet the passage says their systematic effects accumulated year after year, so the claim is well supported.

comprehension.correctAnswer: Time phrases such as by 1948 pin events to their place on the timeline, while discourse markers such as in fact guide the listener through an argument like signposts, so one organises time and the other organises ideas.

comprehension.correctAnswer: His anonymous essay is read aloud in literature class, students begin slipping quotes into conversation, and after his punishment new essays by other writers appear and are passed under desks.

comprehension.question: How does the final scene at the new auditorium prove that Jamal and Miss Imani left a lasting legacy? Use two details from the ending.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The auditorium is named after Miss Imani with the caption She believed in brave breath, and students from every year fill the room with notebooks in hand, showing that the habit of brave speech outlived them both.
comprehension.explanation: An evaluation question linking the closing images of part 2 to the unit's central idea of legacy.

grammar.title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous
grammar.explanation: The Past Simple reports a finished action, while the Past Continuous shows an action in progress across time; used together, they let one event interrupt another in a story.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Past Simple -- regular verbs add -ed: play becomes played, walk becomes walked, finish becomes finished. Irregular verbs take special forms you must memorise: go becomes went, write becomes wrote, find becomes found, have becomes had, see becomes saw.
Past Continuous -- use was (I, he, she, it) or were (you, we, they) with the -ing form: I was writing. They were playing. She was reading.
Use the Past Simple for a completed action: "She led a protest." "He found the notebook."
Use the Past Continuous for an action in progress at a specific time: "She was leading a protest at noon." "They were studying when the bell rang."
Combine them so one action interrupts another: "Jamal was writing an essay when the prefect found his notebook." "While the students were playing football, Jamal slipped behind the assembly hall."
Use two continuous forms for simultaneous actions: "While she was leading the discussion, others were bartering ideas."
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "She lead a protest" instead of "She led a protest", or mixing the pair as in "While she led a protest, others barter supplies"; the background action needs was or were with -ing: "While she was leading a protest, others were bartering supplies."
grammar.memoryTip: Ask whether the action is a snapshot or a film: a finished snapshot takes the Past Simple, while a rolling film of background action takes the Past Continuous.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- complete each sentence with the Past Simple or Past Continuous form: 1) She __________ (lead) a protest while others __________ (barter) supplies. 2) They __________ (play) outside when it __________ (start) to rain. 3) I __________ (watch) a film when my sister __________ (call) me. 4) While the headmaster __________ (speak), the students __________ (whisper) to each other. 5) Jamal __________ (write) in his notebook when the candle __________ (go) out.
Part B -- write two sentences of your own about the story in which one action interrupts another.

grammar.title: The Past Perfect
grammar.explanation: The Past Perfect, formed with had and a past participle, reaches further back than the Past Simple to show which of two past events happened first.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form the Past Perfect with had + past participle. Regular verbs: had played, had walked, had finished. Irregular verbs: had gone, had written, had seen, had eaten.
Structure: subject + had + past participle + the rest of the sentence.
Use it to show that one past action was completed before another: "He had concluded the speech before the defect was revealed." "She had finished her homework before dinner started." "They had left the party when the rain began." "By the time the headmaster arrived, Jamal had already hidden his notebook."
grammar.commonMistake: Using the Past Simple for the earlier of two actions, as in "He concluded the speech before the defect was revealed", which suggests both happened together; write "He had concluded the speech before the defect was revealed" so the order is unmistakable.
grammar.memoryTip: Hear had as a footprint left one step further back in time: whenever it appears, it marks the action that happened first.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- complete each sentence with the Past Perfect: 1) By the time she arrived, I __________ (finish) my book. 2) They __________ (see) the film before it reached the cinema. 3) He __________ (eat) all the biscuits before his friends came over. 4) By the time the bell rang, the students __________ (complete) the test. 5) She __________ (leave) the room before the announcement was made.
Part B -- join each pair with the Past Perfect so the order is clear: 6) Jamal wrote several essays. The headmaster discovered his notebook. (By the time...) 7) Miss Imani read the essay aloud. She realised its power. (Once...)

grammar.title: Reported Speech
grammar.explanation: Reported speech retells what someone said without their exact words, shifting the tense one step back and adjusting pronouns and time expressions.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Follow five steps. 1) Identify the speaker and the statement: She said, "The response is emphatic." 2) Change the pronouns to match who is being discussed. 3) Shift the tense one step back: present simple becomes past simple (is becomes was); present continuous becomes past continuous; past simple becomes past perfect; present perfect becomes past perfect; will becomes would; can becomes could. 4) Add that if you wish. 5) Put it together: She said that the response was emphatic.
Questions use asked + if or whether, or the question word, and lose the question mark: He asked, "Are you coming?" becomes He asked if I was coming. She asked, "Where are you going?" becomes She asked where I was going.
Commands use told + person + to + base verb: "Justify your actions." becomes He told them to justify their actions. "Please close the door." becomes She asked me to close the door.
grammar.commonMistake: Forgetting the tense shift, as in "She said the response is emphatic" instead of "She said that the response was emphatic", or keeping question word order, as in "He asked are you happy" instead of "He asked if I was happy".
grammar.memoryTip: Reporting speech is time travel: step every tense one stage into the past, swap the pronouns, and let the question mark stay behind.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- change each sentence into reported speech: 1) She said, "The game is fun." 2) They asked, "Where are you going?" 3) He told her, "Finish your homework." 4) Jamal said, "I believe in questions." 5) The headmaster asked, "Did you write this?"
Part B -- report these lines from the story: 6) Tariq whispered, "We need to keep this going." 7) Miss Imani said, "This is daring." 8) Amara said, "I do not agree with all this liberal chatter."

grammar.title: Verbs Followed by Prepositions
grammar.explanation: Some verbs need a specific preposition to sound natural and keep their meaning, such as insist on, believe in, waver between and implore for.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Learn the four key combinations for this unit: insist on means to demand firmly ("I insist on finishing my homework before playing."); believe in means to have faith in ("She believes in the power of education."); waver between means to hesitate between options ("He wavered between two choices."); implore for means to beg urgently ("They implored for more time.").
Other common pairs: look at means to see something, while look for means to search for it; depend on means to rely on someone or something; listen to means to pay attention to sounds or a speaker; agree with means to share an opinion; belong to means to be owned by.
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving the preposition out, as in "I insist going to the party", or choosing the wrong one, as in "I believe on fairies"; the correct forms are "I insist on going" and "I believe in fairies".
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the rhyme: insist on a plan, believe in the magic, waver between choices, implore for help when it's tragic.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- fill in the correct preposition (on, in, between or for): 1) I always insist __________ arriving at school on time. 2) Do you believe __________ the importance of reading? 3) She keeps wavering __________ two colours for her project. 4) He implored __________ more time to finish the mural.
Part B -- complete these story sentences: 5) Jamal insisted __________ finishing his essay before sunrise. 6) Tariq believed __________ the power of speaking up. 7) Jamal wavered __________ joining the group and staying safe. 8) The students implored __________ more freedom to discuss ideas.

grammar.title: Phrasal Verbs
grammar.explanation: A phrasal verb joins a verb to a particle to create a completely new meaning, such as get into trouble or ebb away, and these forms fill everyday English.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A phrasal verb has two, or sometimes three, parts: a base verb plus a particle, and the particle changes the meaning. Get alone means to obtain, but get on with means to continue doing something: "Let's get on with the lesson."
Key phrasal verbs for this unit: get into trouble means to find yourself in difficulty ("If you break the rules, you will get into trouble."); ebb away means to decrease or fade gradually ("The excitement began to ebb away."); roil over means to become agitated or disturbed ("His emotions began to roil over.").
Phrasal verbs usually cannot be translated word for word, so learn the meaning of the whole phrase as one unit rather than each word separately.
grammar.commonMistake: Swapping the particle, as in "get on to the lesson" when you mean "get on with the lesson", or translating each word literally from your first language instead of learning the whole phrase's meaning.
grammar.memoryTip: Give each phrasal verb a mental picture, such as a friend trying to get on with homework while a cat keeps jumping onto the desk.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- choose get on with, get into trouble, ebb away or roil over: 1) If you ignore the teacher's warnings, you might __________. 2) After a while, the excitement of the game started to __________. 3) It is important to __________ your work, even when it gets difficult. 4) When I heard the unfair news, my feelings began to __________.
Part B -- write one sentence of your own for each of the four phrasal verbs, using the story or school life as context.

grammar.title: Time Phrases, Reflexive Pronouns and Discourse Markers
grammar.explanation: Time phrases, reflexive pronouns and discourse markers are the finishing tools of narration: they anchor events in time, show self-directed actions and guide the reader between ideas.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Time phrases pin events to the timeline: In those days refers to a past period ("In those days, children played outside for hours."); Eventually means after some time ("Eventually, I learned to be brave."); At the time points to a specific past moment ("At the time, I did not understand why it mattered."); By 1948 means before or at that year ("By 1948, many radios carried news of independence."). Time phrases sit most naturally at the start of a sentence, though they can also close one: "I did not understand it at the time."
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and the object are the same person: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. "She looked at herself in the mirror." "I taught myself how to play the guitar." "He completed the project all by himself." Adding a reflexive can also stress that nobody helped: "I made the cake myself."
Discourse markers connect ideas like signposts, usually at the start of a sentence and followed by a comma: Well shows hesitation or a change of thought; Basically simplifies or summarises; For example introduces a specific case; In fact adds emphasis or surprising information; Actually corrects or adds unexpected information. "Well, I think we should go." "In fact, the test was easier than I expected."
grammar.commonMistake: Using a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object are different people, as in "She gave it to herself" when the gift goes to someone else, and dropping the comma after a discourse marker, as in "Well I think we should go".
grammar.memoryTip: Use T.I.M.E. for time phrases -- Think of the action, Identify the time phrase, Make the sentence, Ensure it fits -- and remember that reflexives are self-action words.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- fill in the correct time phrase (In those days, Eventually, At the time or By 1948): 1) __________, children used to play outside until dark. 2) I wanted to learn to ride a bike. __________, I managed it! 3) __________, I did not know how to cook. 4) __________, many households had radios, and life was changing.
Part B -- fill in the correct reflexive pronoun: 5) Nora baked a cake by __________. 6) The cats are grooming __________ in the sun. 7) I can do this project all by __________. 8) Leo showed __________ how to ride a bike. 9) We can solve this puzzle by __________. 10) Jamal taught __________ to write persuasive essays.
Part C -- choose the correct discourse marker (Actually, In fact, Basically, Well or For example): 11) __________, I really like playing football after school. 12) I enjoy many sports. __________, I love basketball and tennis. 13) __________, we can have a picnic this weekend! 14) __________, I think we should go to the library first. 15) You can improve your English in many ways. __________, try reading a book every week.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: The Rebellion of Silence Retold
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Retell "The Rebellion of Silence" in your own words for two to three minutes without stopping, with an adult or partner listening. Include at least five vocabulary words from the unit, and use the Past Simple for completed events and the Past Continuous for background action. If you are working with a partner, take turns retelling different sections and note one detail the other person missed.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my retelling of The Rebellion of Silence, check my past tenses, and tell me which two story events I explained most clearly.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Legacy Discussion Circle
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Discuss these questions with a partner, a family member or your AI tutor, giving full answers supported by reasons. Who is a historical figure to you -- a grandparent, a community leader or a teacher -- and why do you admire them? Should students be allowed to discuss politics at school? What kind of legacy would you like to leave behind? Finish by explaining what Jamal's line "Speech is breath made brave" means to you.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Lead a legacy discussion with me, ask one follow-up question after each of my answers, and challenge me to support every opinion with a reason.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Reported Speech Role-Play
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Work with a partner. One person speaks a line as a character from the story; the other reports it using reported speech, then you swap roles. Starting lines: Jamal: "I believe in learning and questions." The headmaster: "Debate and politics will be forbidden on school grounds." Tariq: "We need to keep this going." Miss Imani: "You have done something rare." Amara: "I do not agree with all this liberal chatter, but I respect the courage it takes to speak." Model report: Jamal said that he believed in learning and questions.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Role-play story characters with me and check that I shift tenses and pronouns correctly whenever I report your lines.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Mini-Debate with Discourse Markers
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose one topic and argue it for one to two minutes, connecting your ideas with well, basically, in fact, actually and for example: silence is a more powerful protest than shouting; young people have the right to discuss politics at school; one person can change the direction of a whole community; it is better to follow rules even when you disagree with them. Then ask your partner or AI tutor to argue the other side, and respond to one of their points.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Be my debate partner: argue the opposite side of my chosen topic and point out where a discourse marker would improve my flow.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Vocabulary Expert Interview
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose six unit words, such as reprieve, emphatic, connoisseur, abate, barter and disposition. Play the expert while your partner interviews you: for each word, give its meaning, use it in a sentence about the story or school life, and answer one follow-up question in complete sentences. Swap roles for the final two words.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: The Legacy Address
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Prepare and deliver a sustained five- to six-minute address called What We Leave Behind. Open with a time phrase, synthesize evidence from the legacy information text and the story, evaluate how reliable each source of evidence is, address one counterargument, and close with a single emphatic line. Afterwards, answer two follow-up questions from your listener.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my five- to six-minute legacy address, then give feedback on my evidence, my counterargument and my closing line.

writing.title: Writing 1: Narrative Essay -- A Lasting Legacy
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a narrative essay of 200 to 300 words about a person in your community who has made a lasting impact. Describe what they did, why it mattered and what their legacy is. activities.title: Activities 1: Vocabulary in Context -- Story Sentences
activities.instructionsAndItems: Each sentence below is inspired by "The Rebellion of Silence". Complete it with the correct word from this bank: benign, cache, emphatic, strenuous, initiative, banish, profound, waver, systematic, unsightly. 1) Most students saw Jamal as a __________ shadow who would never cause trouble. 2) Tariq and the others had hidden a __________ of newspapers in a biscuit tin. 3) Jamal's tone in his essays was cautious but __________. 4) The week of cleaning classrooms was a __________ punishment. 5) Jamal showed great __________ by starting the essay campaign on his own. 6) The headmaster threatened to __________ any student who disobeyed the rule. 7) Something in Tariq's voice kindled a __________ feeling inside Jamal. 8) Jamal tried not to __________ when the headmaster confronted him. 9) The student essays formed a __________ network, passed from desk to desk. 10) The dormitory blocks were __________, with peeling paint and rusted windows.

activities.title: Activities 2: Match the Word to the Definition

Definitions: a) to fill something up again; b) extremely happy or excited; c) kind and gentle, not harmful; d) expressing something strongly and clearly; e) requiring a lot of effort and energy; f) a hidden store of things; g) to send someone away as punishment; h) not pleasant to look at; i) the ability to start something on your own; j) very deep, with a strong effect.

quizzes.question: What does 'benign' mean?
quizzes.options: A person's usual mood or way of thinking. | A problem or fault in something that makes it not work properly. | Done according to a plan or system; organised and methodical. | Kind and gentle; not harmful or dangerous.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Kind and gentle; not harmful or dangerous.
quizzes.explanation: Benign describes someone or something kind, gentle and harmless, like the smile classmates saw in the quiet boy at the back of the room.

quizzes.question: What does 'reprieve' mean?
quizzes.options: A hidden store of things, often used to keep items safe. | The distance around the edge of a circle. | A temporary break from something difficult or unpleasant. | An argument that opposes or disagrees with another argument.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A temporary break from something difficult or unpleasant.
quizzes.explanation: A reprieve is a temporary break from something difficult, such as a quiet weekend in the middle of an exam season.

quizzes.question: What does 'connoisseur' mean?
quizzes.options: A person who knows a lot about something and can judge its quality. | The ability to start something on your own without being told. | A place where people or animals live. | The quality or character of a sound, or the way someone speaks.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A person who knows a lot about something and can judge its quality.
quizzes.explanation: A connoisseur has studied a subject so closely that they can judge quality with confidence, like an expert taster of fine teas.

quizzes.question: What does 'petulant' mean?
quizzes.options: Extremely happy or excited. | Easily annoyed and often complaining, like a child. | Someone who prefers traditional values and is cautious about change. | Requiring a lot of effort and energy.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Easily annoyed and often complaining, like a child.
quizzes.explanation: A petulant person is easily annoyed and complains like a sulky child, which is why a petulant reply weakens an argument.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Answers in order: 1) benign 2) cache 3) emphatic 4) strenuous 5) initiative 6) banish 7) profound 8) waver 9) systematic 10) unsightly.

Expected forms: justify, justifiably, justification, justifiable; systematic, systematically, system, systematise; conservative, conservatively, conservatism, conserve; exasperate, exasperatingly, exasperation, exasperating; profound, profoundly, profundity. Accept sensible sentences using any two new forms.

Odd ones out: Group 1 petulant, the only negative personality trait; Group 2 replenish, which means to fill up rather than decrease; Group 3 initiative, which is about starting things rather than places or measurements; Group 4 unsightly, which describes appearance rather than intensity or method.

Model answers: 1) Jamal said that he was happy with his essay. 2) While the students were playing football, Jamal wrote an essay. 3) Jamal had finished the essay before the headmaster called him. 4) Herself is the reflexive pronoun, used because the subject and object are the same person. 5) In those days is the time phrase, signalling that the events belong to a period in the past.

Corrected sentences: 1) While Jamal was writing an essay, the prefect found his notebook. 2) Tariq said that they needed to keep that going. 3) By the time the headmaster arrived, Jamal had hidden his notebook. 4) She insists on finishing her homework before dinner. 5) The students taught themselves how to organise a debate. 6) He was reading a book while it was raining outside.

Correct answer: a temporary break from something difficult or unpleasant. A weekend away from revision is a reprieve, not an escape.

Correct answer: easily annoyed and often complaining, like a child. A petulant tone weakens even a strong argument.
